summary: Discusses the CMS signing-time attribute in RPKI signed objects, which gives the purported time of signing. Because RPKI data is fetched through rsync and RRDP, the document updates RFC 6488 on how this attribute should be used and treated.

eli5.summary: Signed papers carry a date of signing. This says that for routing certificates, that date is not trustworthy, and tells software how to treat it.

questions: what is the cms signing-time attribute in rpki
how does rpki switch from rrdp to rsync
what does rfc 9589 change in rfc 6488
subtitle: How RPKI files can carry their signing time as their modification time, so switching from RRDP to rsync does not re-download everything.

tldr.problem: Relying Parties normally fetch RPKI data over RRDP and fall back to rsync when RRDP fails. On the first rsync run, files fetched earlier over RRDP look different to rsync, so unchanged files are needlessly transferred again.
tldr.mechanism: Both repository operators and Relying Parties set each Signed Object file's modification time to the value of the object's CMS signing-time attribute, so rsync sees matching timestamps and sizes. To make this dependable, the signing-time attribute becomes mandatory and the binary-signing-time attribute is disallowed.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6488 is updated so that every RPKI Signed Object MUST carry a signing-time attribute. The document reports that this broke no commonly used trust anchor or Certification Authority.

today: RFC 9589 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6488, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. It makes the CMS signing-time attribute mandatory in RPKI Signed Objects.

sections.title: Why the Signing Time Matters
sections.content:
In the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI), data is published as Signed Objects: Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) content types wrapped in a standard template defined by RFC 6488. That template had an optional CMS signing-time attribute, which records the time at which the issuer signed the object.

When the template was written, rsync was the only way to distribute RPKI repositories. Since then the RPKI Repository Delta Protocol (RRDP, RFC 8182) was developed. Repository operators must still provide rsync, and RRDP is typically deployed alongside it and preferred by default by most Relying Party (RP) implementations. RPs also fall back to rsync when the RRDP service has problems.

This RFC describes how operators and RPs can use the signing-time attribute to cut the cost of that fallback. It also updates RFC 6488 to make the attribute mandatory and to disallow the binary-signing-time attribute.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to get the same files, and sometimes the first way breaks. The files carry a date, and this document says to use that date to avoid fetching things twice.

sections.title: Switching From RRDP to rsync
sections.content:
The document starts from an existing recommendation: to avoid needless retransfers in consecutive rsync runs, operators should keep a file's last modification time unchanged when its content is unchanged. The new idea is to avoid needless transfers on the first use of rsync too, by reusing data already fetched over RRDP.

The text notes that all commonly used RP implementations first try RRDP. If it fails (for example from malformed XML, an expired TLS certificate or an HTTP connection timeout), the RP tries rsync instead.

By default, rsync uses a file's last modification time (mod-time) and its size to decide whether a file needs the full rsync algorithm. If sender and receiver agree on both, the file is assumed identical and left off the transfer list. Matching mod-times therefore save network bandwidth, disk I/O and CPU.
sections.eli5: When you copy files, the computer first compares the date and size of each one. If both match, it assumes they are the same and skips them.

sections.title: Guidance for Operators and Relying Parties
sections.content:
Both sides get one SHOULD. A repository operator writing Signed Objects to a filesystem for rsync publication SHOULD set each file's mod-time to the value of the CMS signing-time attribute inside the object. A Relying Party writing Signed Objects it retrieved over RRDP to a filesystem SHOULD do the same.

With that in place, an RP that synthesized a filesystem hierarchy from RRDP data can synchronize directly into that directory. Alternatively it can sync into a new, empty directory using the rsync --compare-dest=DIR option. rsync then skips any file already present in DIR and identical to the sender's file. DIR should hold the previously fetched and validated data in its original DER-encoded form, so the file size matches.
sections.eli5: Everyone stamps each file with the date it was signed. Then, when the second delivery truck arrives, you only unload the boxes with dates you have not seen.

sections.title: What Public Repositories Contain Today
sections.content:
Before making the attribute mandatory, the authors checked the real data. Analyzing the rpkiviews archives, which hold millions of Signed Objects discovered via the five Regional Internet Registry (RIR) Trust Anchors from 6 June 2022 to 29 January 2024, every Signed Object contained a CMS signing-time attribute. Making it mandatory therefore would not make any commonly used Trust Anchor or subordinate CA non-compliant.

As of 29 January 2024, for 83.8% of Signed Objects the signing-time matched the file's mod-time as seen via rsync. The document concludes that RPs would already see a significant drop in rsync processing if they adopted the strategy above.

In the same period no Signed Object with a binary-signing-time attribute was found, so disallowing that attribute would not break any commonly used Trust Anchor or CA either.
sections.eli5: The authors looked through millions of files and found that all of them already had a signing date. So requiring one would not upset anyone.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 6488
sections.content:
This RFC edits RFC 6488 in several places. The signedAttrs element MUST still include the content-type and message-digest attributes, and now it MUST also include the signing-time attribute. Other signed attributes MUST NOT be included, so the binary-signing-time attribute is no longer allowed.

  • The sentence saying the signing-time attribute MAY be present becomes MUST be present.
  • The sentence saying that its presence or absence MUST NOT affect validity is removed.
  • The section on the binary-signing-time attribute is removed entirely.
  • In the validation checklist, the signed attributes must contain content-type (OID 1.2.840.113549.1.9.3), message-digest (OID 1.2.840.113549.1.9.4) and signing-time (1.2.840.113549.1.9.5), and no others.
  • The reference to RFC 6019 is removed from the informative references of RFC 6488.
sections.eli5: The old rule book said a date was optional. The new rule book says every file must have one, and a second kind of date is banned.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC imposes no requirement that the signing time be correct. It does not provide reliable information on when the signature was produced, and it has no bearing on whether switching between RRDP and rsync works smoothly.

Banning the binary-signing-time attribute also removes an ambiguity. RFC 6019 requires that the signing-time and binary-signing-time attributes, if both are present, give the same date and time, but an object could still carry values that disagree. Allowing a single field for the signing time removes that possibility.
sections.eli5: The date is only a helpful label for skipping repeat copies, not proof of when something was signed. Having just one date on each file means the dates cannot disagree.
